conceptTag: Respond to a competitor's big sale
readerTitle: Your rival just put 40% off on every doorstep. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카펫 청소 업체, 팔레트 제조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 경쟁사의 세일에는 가격표가 아니라 판매 한 건이 남기는 돈과 상대의 다음 수로 대응한다. 가격을 따라 내리지 않고도 지킬 고객을 지킬 수 있다.
misconception: 경쟁사가 크게 할인하면 같이 내려야 고객을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (공헌이익, 할인 시 필요한 판매 증가)

factChecks.note: 이 레슨은 ECO-08-02(할인)과 ECO-08-06(가격 전쟁)의 개념을 적용합니다. 두 레슨의 용어와 정의가 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your rival just put 40% off on every doorstep. Now what?
body: You run a carpet cleaning business. On Monday, a rival leaves flyers across your town: 40% off all carpet cleaning this month.
By Wednesday, your phone is quieter than usual. Two regular customers ask if you'll match. Your gut says cut prices now, before you lose everyone.

image.label: A doorstep flyer shouting 40% off
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 현관 매트 위에 "40% OFF"가 크게 적힌 전단지가 놓여 있고, 옆에는 조용한 휴대폰이 화면을 위로 한 채 있음. 실제 업체 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you respond?
body: A standard living-room job costs $200. The sale runs for one month. What's your first move?

options.text: Match the 40% for the month so nobody leaves
options.feedback: You keep the headline even, but you hand a big **discount** to every customer, including the ones who'd never have switched. And the rival may cut again.

options.text: Keep your price, and give regulars a small extra like free stain treatment
options.feedback: You protect the customers worth keeping at a fraction of the cost of a price cut, and you avoid starting a **price war**.

options.text: Keep your price and do nothing at all
options.feedback: You protect your margin, but you leave loyal customers with no reason to stay when a cheaper offer is on their doorstep.

cards.title: What matching really costs.
body: At 40% off, each job leaves **$30** instead of $110. To earn the same, you'd need about 3.7 times as many jobs. The rival's flyers won't send you that many.

cards.title: A matched price goes to everyone.
body: The lesson on **discounting** showed that a price cut comes straight out of what each sale leaves behind. Here, matching shrinks that by about 73%.

It also goes to the wrong people. Deal hunters chase the flyer and leave again when it ends. Your regulars pay for reliability and trust. If you match, you mostly give money to people who were never going to leave.
A small, targeted extra costs far less and reaches only the customers you want to keep.

cards.title: Matching invites the next cut.
body: A rival who sees you match has two choices: give up the sale, or go deeper. Many go deeper. That's how a **price war** starts, and both sides end up keeping less on every job.
Customers also learn to wait for the next round of discounts.
Answering on something other than price, like speed, guarantees or perks for regulars, gives the rival nothing to hit back at.

image.label: Two price tags sliding down a staircase
image.brief: 두 개의 가격표가 계단을 한 칸씩 번갈아 내려가는 모습. 계단 아래쪽으로 갈수록 가격표가 작아지고 색이 바램. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: When a rival software company cuts its price, the same logic applies. A targeted retention offer to accounts that are about to renew usually costs less than a public price cut for every user.

cards.title: Now you make wooden pallets.
body: You sell pallets to warehouses at $12 each. Wood, nails and delivery cost $9, so each leaves $3. A rival offers your biggest client 15% off for three months.
At $10.20, each pallet would leave $1.20. You'd need 2.5 times the volume to break even. What do you do?

options.text: Cut your price 15% for every client
options.feedback: You'd give up 60% of what each pallet leaves behind across your whole book, to answer one offer to one client. That's the **discounting** trap.

options.text: Offer that client a better rate only in exchange for a longer contract
options.feedback: You meet the threat where it is and get something back for the discount, without changing your list price. It also gives the rival no public price to undercut, avoiding a **price war**.

options.text: Ignore it, since the offer only lasts three months
options.feedback: Holding your price is often right, but a big client who switches may not come back after three months. A quiet conversation is cheap insurance.

cards.title: Sometimes you do have to move.
body: Holding your price works when the rival's sale is temporary and your customers value more than price.

It works less well when the rival has found a lasting cost advantage, when customers see your product as identical to theirs, or when you're losing customers fast. Then waiting just means losing slowly.
So check before you decide. Count who actually left and why, rather than reacting to a flyer.

cards.title: Answer a rival's sale with math, not panic.
body: You used two ideas. **Discounting:** a matched cut costs far more than it looks and goes to customers who'd have stayed. **Price wars:** matching invites the next cut, so answer on something other than the price tag.
**Try it today:** list your five most loyal customers. Write down one inexpensive thing you could offer them that a rival's sale can't.
